The father is himself the hostage being held by the kidnapper. The demand is made over the smartphone to his daughter: she must bring one hundred million yen alone by noon, or the hostage — her father — will be killed.

The father realizes that paying would save him only by making his daughter come alone to the kidnapper. That would put her directly in the kidnapper's hands, and the kidnapper would likely take both the money and her. So by refusing the ransom, the father protects his daughter from being lured into the trap, even though it means risking his own life.

The father is the hostage. The kidnapper, holding the father, phones the daughter and demands that she bring one hundred million yen alone by noon or the father will be killed. Overhearing this, the father decides the ransom must not be paid because the demand requires his daughter to come alone to the kidnapper. He believes that if she does so, the kidnapper will not let either of them go — the money would not secure his release and would instead place his daughter in the kidnapper's power. His refusal is therefore motivated primarily by protecting his daughter from harm, even at the risk of his own life.

The father decides the ransom should not be paid because the payment would require his daughter to come alone into the kidnapper's hands. He believes that if she did so, the kidnapper would not simply release him: the money would not free him, and the daughter would also be seized or harmed. His refusal is thus primarily aimed at protecting his daughter from being lured into the kidnapper's trap, even at the risk of his own life.
